title: Reading slowly
hook: reading for information and reading for formation are different speeds

segments.voice: Yesterday, ner, a lamp for my feet, and your line: a lamp unto my feet. Today, the speed you read at.

The terms and conditions on a new app: scroll, scroll, agree. Now a different page: a letter in a drawer, in the handwriting of someone who has died, found years later. That one gets read slowly. A pause at a phrase. A second reading. One sentence, ten times over, until the voice comes back. Same eyes, same alphabet, completely different reading. Headlines, feeds and emails tend to get the first speed: skimming for what's needed. Some Christian teachers say the Bible is meant to be read, at least sometimes, at the second.
screen: `TERMS AND CONDITIONS: SCROLL, AGREE.` → `A LETTER FOUND IN A DRAWER.` → `TWO SPEEDS OF READING.`

segments.voice: Some Christian writers call the two speeds reading for information and reading for formation. The first asks: what does this say? The second asks: what is this doing to me? Both matter, they say: the first tells you what's there, and the second is where the words start to shape a life. The Bible itself describes the slow kind. The first psalm, the one from three days ago, praises the person whose "delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night." That word meditate, in Hebrew hagah, doesn't mean sitting silent with an empty mind. It means to murmur, to mutter under your breath. Isaiah uses the same word for a lion growling over its prey. So the picture is someone going over the words out loud, again and again, low and slow, like a lion that won't let go. Augustine, in his Confessions, describes watching the bishop Ambrose read with his eyes moving and his voice silent, and wondering why. Some medieval monks called slow reading rumination: chewing on the words the way a cow chews the cud. You met their method on day one hundred one, lectio divina: read, notice a word, ponder, rest. Christians from different churches read this way in some form: monks and nuns, some Protestants with a single verse in a morning quiet time, people who imagine themselves into a Gospel scene. At full speed, the words pass through you. Slowed down, one word can hold you for a whole minute.
screen: `INFORMATION, THEN FORMATION.` · `HAGAH: TO MURMUR.` · `A LION THAT WON'T LET GO.` · `ONE WORD CAN HOLD YOU.`

segments.voice: If you have a Bible, open to Psalm 23 and take the first five verses; if not, its first line: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." Read it once at normal speed, then again twice as slowly, murmuring under your breath, and when one word catches you, stop there and say it again. If you pray, let that word become your prayer; if you don't, just stay with it.
screen: `THE LORD IS MY SHEPHERD; I SHALL NOT WANT.`

segments.voice: Reading slowly. Reading for formation, not only information: murmuring the words until one stops you. Today's word.
Your line: slow down to hear. Information first, then formation. That's one hundred twenty-nine days.

howItsDone: Some Christians read scripture slowly, often aloud or under their breath, repeating a phrase and pausing on a word; monks and nuns practice this as lectio divina, and some Protestants read a single verse slowly in a morning quiet time.

notes: 'Reading for information and reading for formation' is a phrase associated with modern writers (e.g. M. Robert Mulholland); described only as what 'some Christian writers' say. Confirm.
Hagah in Isaiah 31:4 of a lion growling over prey (KJV 'roaring'): confirm.
Augustine's surprise at Ambrose's silent reading (Confessions 6.3): the scene is famous; scholars debate how rare silent reading actually was. Consider a softer note.
Ruminatio as a monastic image: standard. Confirm.
Cross-reference to day 101 (lectio divina) written by another agent; confirm consistent description.
